# What is the academic disagreement on whether scaling laws are evidence for or against AGI on a near-term timeline? Steelman both sides.

*Generated by Blitz-Swarm on 2026-11-04 23:35*

## Assessment

Scaling laws are strong evidence that additional resources can predictably improve language-model prediction loss within studied regimes. They are weaker evidence about general capabilities, and substantially weaker evidence about when AGI will arrive. The academic disagreement concerns the bridges between these propositions: whether lower prediction loss reliably produces the breadth, reliability, autonomy, and adaptability required for AGI, and whether historical relationships survive extrapolation far beyond their measurement range.

The strongest optimistic argument is that repeated, quantitatively predictable improvements across architectures, scales, and tasks provide an empirical development path toward increasingly general competence. The strongest skeptical argument is that this path predicts a training objective, while near-term AGI requires several additional relationships that have not been established. Neither position follows deductively from scaling laws alone.

This account draws on research recalled from knowledge, without live source verification, as requested. It covers foundational work through 2024 and should not be read as an assessment of the latest frontier systems. Paper links identify primary research; most cited papers initially appeared as preprints, and publication or peer review does not establish independent replication.

## 1. What loss-scaling studies actually establish

**Kaplan et al. (2020), *Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models*.** The researchers trained autoregressive Transformers across different parameter counts, dataset sizes, and training budgets, then fitted power-law relationships between those resources and held-out cross-entropy loss. They found substantial regularity and used fitted relationships to derive compute-efficient allocations. Their compute-optimal prescription favored increasing model size more aggressively than training-data volume and stopping training before full convergence. [Primary paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361)

This is consequential empirical evidence: model development can be more predictable than a sequence of isolated engineering breakthroughs. But the fitted dependent variable is average token-prediction loss on a specified distribution. It is neither a direct measure of intelligence nor a calendar-time forecast.

**Hoffmann et al. (2022), *Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models*.** The authors trained more than 400 models spanning approximately 70 million–16 billion parameters and 5–500 billion training tokens. They used several fitting approaches to estimate the allocation of parameters and tokens that minimized loss at a given compute budget. Their preferred prescription increased parameters and tokens approximately equally as compute grew. A larger validation run, Chinchilla, used 70 billion parameters and approximately 1.4 trillion tokens; it outperformed the 280-billion-parameter Gopher, trained on approximately 300 billion tokens, at a comparable training-compute budget. Those numbers describe model and dataset configurations, not a universal performance multiplier. [Primary paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556)

**Why the difference matters:** Kaplan and Hoffmann support the existence of useful scaling relationships while disagreeing materially about the optimal allocation of resources. The disagreement reflects experimental coverage, optimization assumptions, and fitting methods. This is evidence against treating a particular fitted law as a timeless physical law. It is also evidence for a scientific process capable of improving predictive prescriptions through additional experiments.

**Henighan et al. (2020), *Scaling Laws for Autoregressive Generative Modeling*.** Experiments across multiple modalities found further regularities in generative-model loss. This broadens the evidence beyond one language dataset, although shared institutions and methods mean it should not be counted as wholly independent replication. [Primary paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.14701)

**Empirical status:** Smooth loss improvement is a well-supported regularity across many studied settings. Exact exponents, optimal resource allocations, and behavior outside those settings have weaker support. An apparent irreducible-loss term is a fitted property of the model and data setup; it should not automatically be interpreted as either a fundamental ceiling on intelligence or a measured distance to AGI.

## 2. The optimistic bridge: prediction improvement can produce general capability

The optimistic case is stronger than “a graph goes down, therefore AGI.”

First, language prediction requires exploiting structure in human-generated data. Better prediction can reward learning facts, syntax, latent causal relationships, procedural patterns, and representations useful across tasks. The breadth of downstream transfer gives this argument empirical substance, although it does not prove that prediction will supply every component of intelligence.

Second, some downstream performance is predictable. **GPT-4’s technical report (OpenAI, 2023)** describes forecasting final loss from substantially smaller training runs and forecasting performance on a subset of HumanEval programming problems using smaller models. The methodology extrapolated relationships measured in smaller runs to a larger training run, providing an example of a successful forecast rather than merely a retrospective curve fit. [Primary technical report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.08774)

This evidence supports the possibility of capability forecasting. Its limitations are substantial: selected tasks, restricted training disclosure, limited independent reproducibility, and no direct test of AGI. A successful coding forecast does not establish predictable scaling for every capability required by an autonomous scientist or worker.

Third, **BIG-bench (Srivastava et al., 2022)** documented diverse task behavior across model sizes, including gradual improvement and apparently abrupt gains. That breadth makes an explanation based entirely on a single benchmark artifact less plausible. Nevertheless, BIG-bench tasks are researcher-selected probes, rather than a representative sample of all economically or scientifically important activities. [Primary paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.04615)

A sophisticated optimist therefore argues that repeated gains across heterogeneous tasks increase confidence in a broadly useful learning process. This argument need not assume that pretraining alone is sufficient: better base models may make instruction tuning, reinforcement learning, tools, retrieval, and test-time search more effective. However, the contribution of those additions must be measured separately; gains from the whole system cannot automatically be credited to a fixed pretraining scaling law.

## 3. The skeptical bridge objection: loss is an incomplete capability measure

Average cross-entropy aggregates performance over many token contexts. Improving common or predictable contexts can reduce average loss without proportionate improvement on rare but consequential failures. Conversely, a small average-loss change can materially affect a narrow task.

Accordingly, knowing a model’s loss does not uniquely determine its performance on long-horizon planning, unfamiliar environments, causal intervention, or reliable tool use. Data composition, architecture, training procedure, prompting, and evaluation format can change the mapping. This is an identification problem: the same aggregate loss can conceal different capability profiles.

**Caballero et al. (2023), *Broken Neural Scaling Laws*** fit functional forms that allow changes in scaling behavior across regimes, including downstream measures. Their work shows that a single straight line in log-log space can miss important transitions. It does not show that prediction is impossible; rather, successful extrapolation requires specifying and validating the relevant functional form. [Primary paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.14891)

Skeptics can therefore accept the practical success of loss scaling while rejecting strong timeline conclusions. A near-term AGI forecast needs evidence about the particular capabilities that currently constrain general performance, their scaling relationships, and the resources necessary to improve them. Aggregate loss alone does not supply that evidence.

## 4. Emergence: real capability changes versus measurement thresholds

**Wei et al. (2022), *Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models*** characterize abilities that appear absent in smaller models and present in larger ones. Their examples support the possibility that smooth changes in model resources can coincide with practically striking changes in observed task performance. [Primary paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.07682)

**Schaeffer, Miranda, and Koyejo (2023), *Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?*** argue that some apparent discontinuities arise from nonlinear or discontinuous metrics. Their analyses use alternative scoring rules and controlled examples to show how gradual underlying changes can appear abrupt under measures such as exact-match accuracy. [Primary paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.15004)

The mathematical mechanism is straightforward: a task scored only when an entire answer is correct can remain near zero while component-level competence improves, then rise sharply once enough components are reliable. This is an illustration of the measurement issue, not an empirical claim that all tasks have independent components or follow a particular formula.

**Steelman of emergence:** Threshold effects can still matter enormously in practice. A capability becoming useful may be consequential even when its underlying development is continuous. Some task changes may also reflect mechanisms not captured by a simple scoring artifact.

**Steelman of the critique:** Apparent jumps in coarse benchmark scores are insufficient evidence for unpredictable qualitative transitions in cognition. Sparse observations across model sizes and retrospective selection of striking tasks make the inference especially fragile.

These findings do not establish that all emergence is illusory or that future breakthroughs are inevitable. They narrow what a plotted discontinuity can legitimately demonstrate. Smooth latent improvement and abrupt practical usefulness can coexist.

## 5. Why benchmarks do not settle the timeline question

**Contamination and memorization.** Evaluation material or close variants can occur in training data. Unless provenance and overlap are audited, a rising score combines uncertain amounts of transfer and familiarity. Public benchmarks become particularly difficult to interpret after repeated exposure and optimization.

**Construct validity.** Multiple-choice knowledge, short code generation, and competition-style mathematics measure useful abilities, but their relationship to reliable autonomous work is incomplete. A system may perform well on individually specified tasks while failing to formulate goals, notice errors, recover from interruptions, or sustain a project.

**Prompt and evaluation dependence.** Results depend on instructions, examples, sampling, tool availability, and scoring. Scaling comparisons require those conditions to be controlled or explicitly modeled. A stronger scaffold can improve performance while obscuring what changed in the underlying model.

**Saturation and task selection.** A benchmark can stop distinguishing systems before important weaknesses disappear. Conversely, evaluators can continually introduce harder tasks. Benchmark saturation is not sufficient evidence of AGI, and an indefinitely renewable supply of failures is not sufficient evidence against it.

**Robustness under perturbation.** Mirzadeh et al. (2024), *GSM-Symbolic*, evaluated mathematical reasoning using generated variations of problem templates and changes to problem details. Their results indicate that aggregate accuracy can conceal sensitivity to alterations that should preserve much of the reasoning structure. This is primary evidence about the tested models and task family, not a proof of permanent limitations in all language models. [Primary paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.05229)

**Statistical weakness.** For individual capability claims, concerns often include limited task samples, correlated examples, repeated prompt development, and selection of favorable demonstrations. Classical p-hacking and publication bias are possible, but their prevalence cannot be inferred merely from observing a surprising result. The stronger established concern is researcher flexibility and incomplete reporting of evaluation choices.

## 6. Do historical fits justify extrapolation?

Historical fits justify some extrapolation, with confidence depending on distance and experimental stability. Their strongest use is interpolation or limited extrapolation within a comparable architecture, data distribution, training recipe, and evaluation protocol. Prospective forecasts are stronger evidence than explanations fitted after seeing the outcome.

An AGI timeline requires several additional mappings:

1. **Resources to loss:** how compute, data, architecture, and optimization affect prediction quality.
2. **Loss and training procedure to capability:** how those improvements affect the abilities that constrain general competence.
3. **Capability to an operational AGI threshold:** what breadth, reliability, independence, and adaptability count as success.
4. **Calendar time to available resources:** what hardware, investment, data, and engineering progress will actually materialize.

The first mapping has the strongest direct empirical foundation. The others have partial evidence and substantial uncertainty. Confidence in a fitted loss curve cannot simply be transferred to the final timeline.

A further distinction is essential: scaling studies commonly measure final performance after a controlled training process. They do not, by themselves, demonstrate that a deployed model learns new skills continuously, experiments effectively in the world, or improves its own learning algorithm. Those possibilities need separate tests.

## 7. Steelmanning the opposing conclusions

### Scaling laws support a near-term AGI hypothesis

The strongest case is cumulative: broad learning objectives have yielded transferable capabilities; predictable loss improvements have survived major increases in scale; some capability forecasts have succeeded prospectively; and useful performance can appear after crossing thresholds. If the capabilities currently limiting generality also respond to more compute, better data, post-training, and inference-time computation, AGI might require further development of an existing approach rather than a wholly new principle.

This makes scaling evidence relevant to near-term AGI. It weakens categorical arguments that the approach cannot yield general capabilities. However, neither the compute threshold nor the arrival date follows from the foundational scaling papers. Near-term optimism still rests on assumptions about unmeasured capabilities and available resources.

### Scaling laws undermine confidence in a near-term AGI hypothesis

The strongest skeptical case accepts the observed gains but emphasizes their limits: fitted relationships can change; optimization prescriptions have been revised; downstream behavior is task- and metric-dependent; and benchmark success under controlled conditions does not establish reliable open-ended agency. If critical capabilities improve much more slowly than average prediction loss, impressive aggregate progress could coexist with a distant AGI threshold.

Power laws also involve diminishing improvements in the measured loss for successive absolute increments of resources. But that observation alone is not evidence that AGI is far away: the practical consequence depends on the loss-to-capability relationship and where the relevant threshold lies. A serious skeptical forecast needs measured bottlenecks or resource constraints, rather than diminishing returns alone.

## Conclusion

The strongest evidence supports predictable improvement of particular objectives and a substantial, imperfect relationship between scale and useful capability. It does not establish a universal capability curve or an AGI arrival date. Scaling laws favor continued progress more clearly than they favor a particular near-term timeline. The decisive unresolved question is whether the abilities required for reliable general autonomy follow the same tractable scaling relationships as the losses and benchmarks already measured.

### Scope and central judgment

The strongest skeptical position is **not that scaling laws have stopped working**. It is that predictable improvement in a training objective does not establish a predictable arrival date for broadly competent, reliable autonomous intelligence. Scaling laws provide evidence about an optimization process; forecasting near-term AGI additionally requires a defensible mapping from training loss to general capability, an account of resource availability, and evidence that remaining failures yield to feasible increases in scale.

Here, “near-term AGI” means a system arriving within the next several years that can learn and perform a wide range of cognitively demanding tasks with substantial autonomy. Different definitions materially change the argument. A system that answers most benchmark questions is a weaker target than one that reliably completes unfamiliar projects.

This analysis draws on literature known through 2024. Sources and publication details have not been checked live, so it should not be treated as an assessment of developments after that period.

### 1. Scaling laws predict loss more directly than intelligence

**Primary evidence.** Kaplan et al. (2020), *Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models*, fit empirical relationships between language-model cross-entropy loss and model size, dataset size, and training compute. Hoffmann et al. (2022), *Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models*, revised the allocation of compute between parameters and training tokens. Their study trained more than 400 models spanning approximately 70 million–16 billion parameters and 5–500 billion training tokens, then tested the resulting allocation prescription with Chinchilla: a 70-billion-parameter model trained on 1.4 trillion tokens. These were controlled training experiments and empirical curve fits, not measurements of an AGI threshold. [Kaplan et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361), [Hoffmann et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556).

**Skeptical interpretation.** Cross-entropy averages prediction quality across a token distribution. It does not directly measure whether a system can formulate a new scientific hypothesis, recover from an unexpected tool failure, or carry out a complicated project. An improvement in average prediction can coexist with persistent failures in rare but decisive situations. Even an excellent loss forecast leaves the loss-to-AGI relationship unidentified.

This is a problem of inference, not evidence that prediction is irrelevant to intelligence. Rich prediction clearly requires useful representations. The skeptical objection is that the required representations, their robustness, and the threshold for autonomous competence have not been established by the scaling curves themselves.

**Strong opposing response.** The predictive objective has repeatedly produced capabilities beyond superficial text imitation. The emergence of useful transfer across tasks makes continued generalization a reasonable empirical hypothesis. A scaling advocate need not claim that loss literally measures intelligence; they can argue that it is a useful leading indicator.

**Assessment.** This is the strongest skeptical point. Existing scaling laws support continued improvement more securely than any particular AGI deadline.

### 2. Diminishing returns can make a successful scaling law economically discouraging

For an illustrative power law, let reducible loss be \(L(C)-L_\infty=A C^{-\alpha}\), where \(C\) denotes compute. Reducing that component of loss by a factor \(r\) requires multiplying compute by \(r^{1/\alpha}\). This is an algebraic implication of the assumed model, not an empirical estimate of the cost of AGI.

**Skeptical interpretation.** Smooth progress and diminishing marginal returns are compatible. A straight line on a log–log plot can conceal increasingly expensive absolute gains. If the capability threshold is far away, a highly predictable curve can imply an impractical resource requirement. Moreover, neither the relevant irreducible loss nor the AGI threshold is known well enough to make this calculation decisive.

**Strong opposing response.** The relevant object is capability per dollar, not loss per floating-point operation alone. Hardware, algorithms, data quality, inference methods, and software can improve together. A small reduction in average loss might also cross an important capability threshold.

**Assessment.** Diminishing returns undermine the claim that continued scaling makes near-term AGI inevitable. They do not establish that useful capability gains are diminishing at the same rate.

### 3. Data constraints weaken straightforward extrapolation

**Primary evidence.** Hoffmann et al. showed that compute-efficient training requires increasing training data alongside model size. Muennighoff et al. (2023), *Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models*, experimentally examined repeated-data training and found that reuse has limits rather than behaving indefinitely like additional fresh data. Villalobos et al. (2024), *Will We Run Out of Data? Limits of LLM Scaling Based on Human-Generated Data*, estimated the available stock of public human-generated text and compared it with projected training demand. Their depletion estimates are scenario-dependent forecasts, not observations of an exhausted resource. [Muennighoff et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16264), [Villalobos et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.04325).

**Skeptical interpretation.** Public text is finite, uneven in quality, duplicated, and incomplete as a record of human knowledge. Practical availability is further reduced by access restrictions and collection costs. More fundamentally, language corpora may undersupply the interactive evidence needed for physical reasoning, experimentation, and learning the consequences of actions.

Synthetic data is not an automatic escape. Shumailov et al. (2024), *AI Models Collapse When Trained on Recursively Generated Data*, demonstrated degradation in recursive training settings, including loss of distributional tails. The proposed concern is that generating more examples from a model need not add independent information, and can amplify its omissions. [Shumailov et al.](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07566-y).

**Limits and opposing response.** Model collapse does not establish that all synthetic data is harmful. Results depend on replacement versus retention of real data, filtering, and the training process. Code execution, mathematical verification, simulators, and interaction can supply feedback beyond the generating model's unsupported judgments. A public-text bottleneck is therefore evidence against indefinite repetition of one training recipe, not against every scaling strategy.

### 4. Compute constraints are real, but there is no demonstrated universal wall

**Skeptical interpretation.** Extrapolating training compute requires extrapolating investment, accelerator manufacturing, memory, networking, electricity, and construction. These are interacting industrial constraints. Hardware efficiency does not automatically translate into proportionate growth in usable training compute, and large distributed runs introduce communication and reliability costs.

A separate issue is deployment economics. A system might become capable with extensive sampling, tool use, or search but remain too costly for broad substitution of human work. Training feasibility and economical operation are different questions.

**Strong opposing response.** Industrial constraints can move as investment responds to demand. Algorithmic efficiency, specialization, and inference-time computation can alter the resource requirement substantially. Historical improvements in compute efficiency make a fixed current-cost extrapolation unreliable.

**Assessment.** Resource constraints justify scenario analysis and wider timeline uncertainty. They do not currently supply an established physical or economic theorem excluding near-term AGI. Claims of a specific hard deadline or unavoidable compute wall need more evidence than general references to energy demand.

### 5. Reliability can lag behind average task performance

**Primary evidence.** The HELM evaluation framework measures multiple dimensions, including accuracy, calibration, robustness, and efficiency, illustrating why a single aggregate score is insufficient (Liang et al., 2023). Turpin et al. (2023), *Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think*, experimentally introduced biasing features into prompts and found cases where generated explanations failed to disclose the factors influencing answers. Such findings weaken the use of fluent reasoning traces as direct evidence of dependable reasoning. [HELM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.09110), [Turpin et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.04388).

**Skeptical interpretation.** Autonomous work requires sustained correctness, detection of mistakes, and successful recovery. As an illustration, if each of 100 indispensable steps independently succeeds with probability 0.99, complete success is approximately 0.366. This is a hypothetical calculation, not an observed agent failure rate. Real errors may be correlated, and real workflows may permit recovery.

The substantive concern is that improved average accuracy does not by itself demonstrate reliable long-horizon execution. Verification can help, but verifying an open-ended scientific or managerial decision can be almost as demanding as making it.

**Strong opposing response.** Independence and irreversible failure are often unrealistic assumptions. Agents can check intermediate results, retry, use tools, and ask for assistance. Human organizations also achieve reliability through processes rather than flawless individual cognition.

**Assessment.** Reliability is a serious missing link between benchmark performance and autonomous AGI, but existing failures are not proof that scaling plus verification cannot close it.

### 6. Reasoning and planning expose limits that next-token loss can obscure

**Primary evidence.** Dziri et al. (2023), *Faith and Fate: Limits of Transformers on Compositionality*, studied structured tasks with controllable compositional complexity. Their experiments found important failures as complexity increased, supporting concern about brittle generalization beyond familiar problem structures. Valmeekam et al. (2023), *On the Planning Abilities of Large Language Models: A Critical Investigation*, evaluated planning in formally specified environments with checkable solutions, reporting substantial weaknesses in generating executable plans. [Dziri et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18654), [Valmeekam et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.15771).

**Skeptical interpretation.** Producing a plausible description of a plan is different from maintaining an accurate state representation, respecting constraints, and searching for an executable sequence of actions. Greater familiarity with solution patterns may improve benchmark scores without yielding robust generalization to longer or structurally unfamiliar tasks.

This motivates the claim that external memory, explicit search, learned world models, interaction, or different training objectives may be needed. It does not establish which addition is necessary or whether any constitutes a fundamental architectural break.

**Methodological limits.** These studies evaluate particular models, prompts, and task distributions. Artificial puzzles can isolate a weakness while overstating its relevance to ordinary work. Conversely, familiar benchmark tasks can conceal weaknesses through contamination or pattern familiarity. Failures by older models cannot establish an immutable limitation of later systems.

**Strong opposing response.** The scalable system need not be a single unaided forward pass. Search, tools, reinforcement learning, and inference-time computation may convert a model's partial competence into reliable solutions. Snell et al. (2024), *Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally Can Be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters*, provides experimental evidence that allocating additional inference computation can improve mathematical problem solving under studied conditions. Generalization to arbitrary planning remains unestablished. [Snell et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.03314).

### 7. Apparent emergence and failure both require careful measurement

Schaeffer, Miranda, and Koyejo (2023), *Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?*, showed that discontinuous metrics can produce apparently abrupt capability changes from smoother underlying improvements. This challenges some arguments that benchmark jumps establish an impending general-intelligence transition. It does not show that all qualitative transitions are artifacts. [Schaeffer et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.15004).

Conversely, McKenzie et al. (2023), *Inverse Scaling: When Bigger Isn't Better*, documented tasks where larger models performed worse, with some trends reversing under further scaling or changed prompting. This cautions against treating either a temporary failure or a temporary success as a universal law. The challenge tasks were selected to expose failures, so they do not estimate the prevalence of inverse scaling across ordinary tasks. [McKenzie et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.09479).

### Overall steelman

The skeptical case is a conjunction: loss improvements have diminishing returns; accessible data and compute cannot be extrapolated without constraints; and reliable reasoning, planning, and autonomy have not been shown to follow a predictable curve toward AGI. Therefore, scaling laws alone are inadequate evidence for a confident near-term arrival forecast.

The strongest opposing case is also empirical: increasingly general capabilities have repeatedly emerged from broadly similar learning methods; resource efficiency continues to improve; and tools, search, feedback, and additional inference computation expand what a scaled model can do. Present limitations may be engineering problems rather than evidence of an approaching fundamental ceiling.

**The defensible disagreement is about extrapolation, sufficiency, and the burden of proof.** The cited literature supports substantial uncertainty about near-term AGI more strongly than it supports either an imminent-AGI conclusion or a proof that current approaches cannot get there.

## Central finding

Scaling laws provide substantial evidence that additional resources can predictably improve particular learning objectives. They do **not independently establish an AGI arrival date**. The academic disagreement concerns the bridge from predictive performance to general competence, and from resource requirements to calendar time. The strongest optimistic argument is a conditional extrapolation; the strongest skeptical argument identifies missing capabilities or resource constraints that could invalidate that extrapolation. Neither constitutes a demonstrated theorem about AGI timelines.

This synthesis draws principally on literature published in 2019–2024; it is not a comprehensive assessment of developments through late 2026.

## Definitions change the forecast target

**Broad task performance:** Morris et al. (2024), an ICML position paper, distinguish breadth of competence from performance level and treat autonomy separately. Their proposed Competent AGI threshold requires performance at least at the median of skilled adults across a wide range of nonphysical tasks, including metacognitive abilities such as learning new skills. This is a proposed operational framework, not a validated measurement instrument or an academic consensus. Its percentile is a definitional threshold, not an empirical result. [Morris et al., 2024](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v235/morris24b.html)

**Efficient acquisition of unfamiliar skills:** Chollet (2019) defines intelligence through skill-acquisition efficiency, accounting for priors, experience, scope and generalization difficulty. Under this conception, better performance after vastly more training does not by itself establish greater general intelligence. This is a conceptual and benchmark-design argument, not proof that scaling cannot produce efficient generalization. [Chollet, 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.01547)

**Comprehensive human replacement:** Grace et al. (2024) investigate high-level machine intelligence and full automation of human occupations as separate forecast targets. Neither should be silently substituted for a broad cognitive-performance definition of AGI. Embodied work, economic feasibility and autonomy introduce additional requirements. [Grace et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.02843)

**Near-term:** There is no universally accepted academic interval. For this analysis, an explicit illustrative target is AGI within ten years of this task's date, by November 2036. That is an analytical convention, not a scientific estimate. Historical predictions must retain their original dates; a forecast made in 2023 about the next decade cannot be continually moved forward.

## What the scaling evidence establishes

Kaplan et al. (2020) fit empirical relationships between language-model cross-entropy loss and parameter count, dataset size and training compute. Some fitted trends span more than seven orders of magnitude in the relevant resources. These experiments establish regularities in predictive loss within investigated training regimes; they do not identify a human-general-intelligence loss threshold. [Kaplan et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361)

Hoffmann et al. (2022), published at NeurIPS, trained over 400 models spanning 70 million to over 16 billion parameters and 5–500 billion training tokens. Their allocation analyses indicated that compute-optimal parameter count and training tokens should grow approximately together. They tested the allocation prescription using Chinchilla, a 70-billion-parameter model trained with the same compute budget as the larger Gopher model. This is meaningful prospective validation of resource allocation and downstream improvement. It remains a test of a training prescription, not an AGI forecast. [Hoffmann et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556)

The distinction matters: multiple studies support the broad phenomenon, while particular fitted prescriptions can change with experimental design, optimization and the resource regime.

## Steelman: evidence against near-term AGI

The strongest skeptical case accepts the measured scaling relationships but questions whether the measured objective captures the limiting requirements of AGI. Average predictive loss can improve while unfamiliar-task learning, causal intervention, dependable planning or error recovery remain inadequate. Under Chollet's definition, improvements in learned repertoire are particularly incomplete evidence about efficient acquisition of new skills.

Controlled generalization failures provide more substantive evidence than philosophical objections alone. Berglund et al. (2023; revised 2024) fine-tuned autoregressive models on fictitious factual statements and tested the reverse relationship. Their reversal-curse experiments exposed failures to transfer learned information in that direction across tested model families and sizes. Crucially, the authors also note that models can infer reverse relationships when the premise is supplied in context. These results challenge an uncomplicated claim that ordinary training automatically produces systematic knowledge, while leaving open alternative training and inference methods. They do not establish a permanent limitation or a minimum delay to AGI. [Berglund et al., 2023/2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.12288)

Resource availability supplies a distinct route to longer timelines. Villalobos et al. (2024 revision) estimate the stock of public human-generated text and extrapolate demand from training trends. Their conditional projection places datasets comparable to that stock between 2026 and 2032. This is a modeled supply constraint, not an observed exhaustion date or an AGI impossibility result. The paper explicitly discusses synthetic data, transfer and efficiency improvements as potential ways forward. [Villalobos et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.04325)

To become evidence specifically against the November 2036 target, these concerns require additional support: the missing capability must be necessary under the chosen definition, and its likely remedy or required resources must fall beyond that deadline. A demonstrated weakness today does not supply that calendar-time argument by itself.

## Insufficient support is different from contrary evidence

Let H mean that the agreed AGI criterion is achieved by the agreed deadline. An observation supports H when it is more expected under H than under its alternatives; it counts against H when it is less expected under H.

Consequently:

- Predictable language-loss improvements can favor a scaling-based route relative to a prediction that useful learning would already have stalled, while scarcely distinguishing AGI within a decade from AGI several decades later.
- The absence of an established mapping from loss to general competence undermines confidence in a precise forecast. It does not itself demonstrate that the forecast is false.
- Repeated failure on preregistered, necessary capabilities would count against a specified near-term scaling forecast if that forecast predicted improvement under the tested resources and methods.
- A plateau for one fixed recipe is stronger evidence against that recipe than against every possible near-term AGI development pathway.

The emergence controversy illustrates this distinction. Schaeffer, Miranda and Koyejo (2023), published at NeurIPS, use mathematical analysis, re-evaluation of model outputs, a BIG-Bench meta-analysis and vision experiments to show how metric choices can generate apparent discontinuities. This weakens an argument that mysterious capability jumps establish imminent AGI. It does not show that the underlying improvements are absent; smoother curves could even make forecasting easier. [Schaeffer et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.15004)

## Assumptions that convert scaling into dates

A defensible forecast must expose at least these assumptions:

1. **Target:** Which tasks, human comparison group, learning conditions, reliability level and degree of autonomy constitute AGI?
2. **Capability mapping:** How do improvements in measured objectives translate into those requirements, especially the weakest required capabilities?
3. **Resource threshold:** What compute, data and inference expenditure are sufficient, with what uncertainty?
4. **Resource trajectory:** When can those resources actually be supplied and afforded?
5. **Research dependence:** Which advances beyond a fixed training recipe are assumed, and how long might they take?
6. **Validation and deployment:** Does the target mean a laboratory demonstration, repeatable independent performance or economically usable automation?

Survey evidence demonstrates disagreement, not the correctness of a mechanism. Grace et al. surveyed 2,778 AI researchers in fall 2023. Their aggregate forecasts assigned a 10% probability by 2027 and 50% by 2047 to unaided machines outperforming humans in every possible task, conditional on undisrupted scientific progress. Full occupational automation received substantially later aggregate dates. These are elicited beliefs aggregated across respondents, not frequencies measured in experiments, and the whole sample should not be assumed to have answered every individual item. Nonresponse, framing and uncertain forecasting calibration limit interpretation. [Grace et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.02843)

## Observations that could resolve disagreement

The most informative evidence would be preregistered forecasts of capabilities at the next resource scale, followed by independent evaluations on private, newly constructed tasks. Evaluators should measure unfamiliar-skill acquisition, transfer under changed conditions, sustained autonomous performance and recovery from errors, alongside ordinary benchmark scores.

Experiments should separately vary pretraining, inference expenditure, tools, interaction and post-training. Human comparisons should disclose relevant preparation and assistance. Both continuous progress metrics and complete-task success matter: partial improvement can reveal a trend, while reliable completion determines practical competence.

Persistent forecast failures across well-optimized methods would strengthen skepticism about the specified route. Accurate prospective predictions extending to novel learning and sustained autonomy would strengthen the near-term case. Neither side should be allowed to redefine the target or add unspecified breakthroughs after observing the outcome.

The evidence base remains uneven: resource-to-loss relationships have stronger empirical support than resource-to-AGI or resource-to-calendar-time relationships. Mitchell and Krakauer's peer-reviewed synthesis describes the associated disagreement over understanding, but is a review and conceptual analysis rather than an experiment estimating AGI arrival. Benchmark selection, contamination, sparse frontier observations and unpublished failures remain threats; the sources considered here do not establish that p-hacking or publication bias explains the literature. [Mitchell and Krakauer, 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.13966)

## 1. What the foundational scaling laws establish

**Kaplan et al. (2020), _Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models_.** Controlled training experiments varied model size, dataset size, and computational budget, finding approximately power-law relationships with held-out cross-entropy. Their fitted exponents were approximately 0.076 for parameter count, 0.095 for dataset size, and 0.050 for compute along the compute-efficient frontier. These describe distinct experimental regimes and should not be combined as though they were independent causal coefficients in one equation.

The small compute exponent means loss improves slowly as resources increase. That observation supports two different interpretations:

- Optimists emphasize predictability: a shallow but persistent relationship supplies an engineering route to further progress.
- Skeptics emphasize cost: proportional reductions in the modeled loss require increasingly large resource commitments, and the law supplies no AGI threshold.

Neither interpretation licenses equating a percentage reduction in cross-entropy with the same percentage increase in intelligence. Cross-entropy is measured over a token distribution; intelligence has no corresponding universally accepted scalar.

**Hoffmann et al. (2022), _Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models_.** The authors trained more than 400 models, spanning approximately 70 million–16 billion parameters and 5 billion–500 billion training tokens, and estimated compute-optimal allocations using several fitting approaches. Their central prescription was to increase parameter count and training tokens approximately together as compute grows, materially revising Kaplan et al.'s allocation prescription.

Their large-scale validation compared Chinchilla, with 70 billion parameters trained on approximately 1.4 trillion tokens, against Gopher, with 280 billion parameters trained on approximately 300 billion tokens. At approximately the same training-compute budget, Chinchilla performed better across a broad evaluation suite.

**Interpretation:** this is strong evidence that scaling relationships can guide consequential engineering decisions. It also shows that fitted prescriptions depend on the experimental design, training regime, and allocation assumptions. The revision supports neither “scaling failed” nor “the original extrapolation was certain.” The broad regularity survived while an important quantitative recommendation changed.

**Methodological limits.** These are unusually systematic experiments, but their models, data, objectives, optimizers, and evaluations occupy restricted regions of the possible design space. Models trained under a common recipe are not independent replications across fundamentally different learning systems. Estimated asymptotic loss, fitted exponents, and the selected fitting range can materially influence extrapolation.

## 2. Prediction loss and downstream capability have a real but incomplete connection

The optimistic case does not rest only on falling loss. Larger and better-trained language models have improved across heterogeneous language, knowledge, mathematics, and programming evaluations.

**Brown et al. (2020), _Language Models are Few-Shot Learners_,** evaluated a family of autoregressive models on numerous tasks under zero-, one-, and few-shot prompting. The experiments support broad transfer from a shared training objective, while also documenting task variation and persistent weaknesses. Broad transfer makes language-model loss more relevant to general competence than a narrow supervised training score would be.

**OpenAI (2023), _GPT-4 Technical Report_,** provides a particularly relevant prospective forecasting example. The authors report predicting GPT-4's final loss on an internal code dataset using models trained with up to approximately 10,000 times less compute. They also report forecasting performance on a subset of HumanEval programming problems using models trained with up to approximately 1,000 times less compute. These are different forecasts with different evaluation targets.

This is evidence that some downstream behavior can be forecast from smaller runs. It is not evidence that all downstream capabilities, or AGI itself, share a validated compute threshold. The report is an industry technical report with limited disclosure of the full training setup; its internal loss evaluation is less independently auditable than a fully public replication.

**Why the mapping remains incomplete:** average loss weights tokens according to their frequency in an evaluation distribution. A rare failure involving planning, uncertainty, or tool use may contribute little to average loss while determining whether an autonomous project succeeds. Two systems with similar average loss can also differ in prompting sensitivity, calibration, retrieval, and robustness.

The relevant empirical question is therefore not simply whether loss and capability correlate. It is whether the relationship remains stable for the specific capabilities required by the chosen AGI definition, especially under distribution shift and prolonged interaction.

## 3. Emergence does not settle the disagreement

**Wei et al. (2022), _Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models_,** collected examples in which smaller models performed near chance while larger models achieved substantially better measured performance. Their operational definition concerned an ability that was absent in smaller models and present in larger ones; it did not establish a new physical phase transition or a universal mechanism.

**Schaeffer, Miranda, and Koyejo (2023), _Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?_,** showed how discontinuous or nonlinear metrics, combined with sparse measurements, can produce apparently abrupt emergence. Their empirical reanalyses and mathematical examples support this explanation for the cases examined.

A simple mathematical illustration clarifies the issue. If a task requires every step to be correct and each step succeeds independently with probability p, whole-task success is p raised to the number of steps. Smooth improvements in step accuracy can yield sharply changing task success. This is an illustration, not a measured law of language-model reasoning; real errors are often dependent.

**Steelman for optimism:** smooth underlying improvement can cross practical thresholds that unlock valuable behavior. A capability can become economically or operationally useful without a discontinuity in the underlying learning process. The metric critique therefore does not erase the significance of observed improvements.

**Steelman for skepticism:** an apparent jump is not evidence for an impending sequence of unpredictable breakthroughs culminating in AGI. Thresholds depend on task length, scoring, baseline performance, and the density of tested model sizes. Selected striking examples do not establish how frequently new capabilities will appear.

The defensible synthesis is that some apparent emergence is explained by measurement choices, while practically consequential capability transitions remain real. Neither paper establishes that every claimed emergence is an artifact or that emergence supplies an AGI timeline.

## 4. Benchmark progress is evidence, but its interpretation is limited

**Srivastava et al. (2023), _Beyond the Imitation Game: Quantifying and Extrapolating the Capabilities of Language Models_,** introduced BIG-bench and documented heterogeneous scaling behavior across a diverse collection of tasks. This helps counter inference from a single benchmark, but an aggregate score can still conceal uneven competence.

**Liang et al. (2023), _Holistic Evaluation of Language Models_,** evaluated models across multiple scenarios and metrics, emphasizing that accuracy alone does not capture robustness, calibration, fairness, and efficiency. These additional dimensions matter when benchmark competence is used as evidence for deployable general intelligence.

Four limitations are especially consequential:

1. **Contamination and repeated adaptation.** Public benchmark material can enter training data, and benchmark familiarity can influence model development. Contamination must be investigated; it should not be presumed to explain every result.
2. **Construct validity.** Success on examinations or short coding tasks measures important skills, but does not directly measure learning unfamiliar workflows or reliably completing extended projects.
3. **Evaluation protocol.** Prompting, sampling, retries, tools, and answer aggregation change performance. A score obtained with many attempts is a different quantity from single-attempt reliability.
4. **Selection and saturation.** Researchers and developers preferentially report interesting tasks and successful interventions. Saturated benchmarks cease to distinguish systems, while new benchmarks change the measurement instrument.

These weaknesses reduce the precision of AGI inferences; they do not imply that benchmark progress is empty. The optimistic case strengthens when improvements replicate on private or newly constructed tasks, under controlled inference budgets, and across genuinely different task families.

## 6. The strongest opposing positions

**The strongest near-term optimistic position:** training objectives that reward prediction over sufficiently diverse data encourage broadly useful internal representations. Broad transfer, successful resource-allocation predictions, and some prospective capability forecasts jointly make continued capability gains more credible than speculation without an empirical learning curve. Tools, feedback, interaction, and inference-time computation may complement pretraining. If remaining weaknesses diminish through these mechanisms within attainable budgets, near-term AGI is plausible.

This argument has genuine evidential force: observed generalization and forecasting success should update beliefs. Its weakest step is the claim that the remaining requirements for reliable general autonomy will yield within a particular feasible resource range. Foundational scaling papers do not measure that threshold.

**The strongest skeptical position:** the established laws predict an aggregate objective, while AGI requires a particular collection of capabilities and reliability properties. Scaling measurements have not established a stable, affordable mapping from loss to that collection. Historical forecasting successes warrant confidence in related outcomes, not automatic confidence in unprecedented autonomy. Near-term certainty is therefore underdetermined by the empirical record.

This skepticism is strongest as a criticism of confidence and timing. It becomes weaker when it claims that current failures demonstrate permanent architectural limits or that diminishing returns alone rule out AGI. Those conclusions also require evidence beyond the scaling laws.

**Overall:** scaling laws are evidence for a productive route to more capable systems. They are stronger evidence against claims that progress is wholly unpredictable than against skepticism about a specific AGI date. Their relevance to near-term AGI depends principally on the still-incomplete empirical mapping from prediction improvement to broad, reliable autonomous competence.

## Scope and strongest optimistic claim

The strongest near-term AGI case is a **convergence argument**: continued training scale, more efficient learning, broad transfer, and computation spent on reasoning and verification could jointly produce broadly capable systems without a fundamentally new scientific breakthrough. Scaling laws contribute by making some components of this trajectory empirically predictable. They do not themselves establish either AGI's feasibility or its arrival date.

Here, near-term means approximately the next decade; this is a forecast horizon, not a measured result. AGI means broad competence across unfamiliar cognitive tasks, with learning and reliable execution included. Conclusions are substantially more optimistic under a benchmark-performance definition than under a sustained-autonomy definition. The discussion below uses established literature through 2024, recalled without live verification; it does not assess subsequent frontier developments.

## 1. Training scale supplies a repeatable development path

**Primary evidence:** Kaplan et al. (2020), [*Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361), fit relationships between language-model cross-entropy loss, model size, dataset size, and computation using controlled training experiments. Hoffmann et al. (2022), [*Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556), revised the resource-allocation prescription using a large experimental sweep.

Hoffmann and colleagues trained the 70-billion-parameter Chinchilla on approximately 1.4 trillion tokens and compared it with the 280-billion-parameter Gopher, trained on approximately 300 billion tokens, at approximately the same training-compute budget. Chinchilla performed better across their reported downstream evaluation suite. These are actual model-training and benchmark comparisons, rather than an AGI forecast.

**Optimistic interpretation:** apparent limits of an existing model can reflect inefficient allocation of resources rather than exhaustion of the learning paradigm. Predictable loss improvement, combined with observed downstream improvements, gives laboratories a practical route for further progress.

**Strong skeptical reply:** compute-optimal prediction is not necessarily compute-optimal autonomy, and these experiments do not measure the distance to AGI. The change from Kaplan's prescription to Chinchilla also shows why a fitted scaling relationship should not be treated as an invariant technological roadmap.

**Assessment:** strong evidence for continued improvement within studied settings; indirect evidence for near-term AGI.

## 2. Algorithmic progress makes a fixed-compute extrapolation too pessimistic

**Primary evidence:** Hernandez and Brown (2020), [*Measuring the Algorithmic Efficiency of Neural Networks*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.04305), reconstructed the computation needed by successive image-classification methods to reach AlexNet-level ImageNet performance. They reported a roughly 44-fold reduction in required training computation between 2012 and 2019. The methodology holds a particular performance target approximately fixed and compares the computation of methods reaching it.

**Optimistic interpretation:** capability depends on effective computation, which can increase through hardware, architectures, optimization, data selection, and training procedures. Forecasts based solely on increasing the cost of today's recipe can therefore overstate the resources needed for future capabilities. Chinchilla provides a separate language-model example of improving the capability obtained from an existing budget.

**Limits:** the ImageNet finding is task-specific and retrospective. It does not establish an equivalent improvement rate for language models, general reasoning, or autonomous work. Improvements measured at a fixed old target need not transfer to the frontier. Data curation and development costs can also fall outside a narrow training-FLOP accounting.

The defensible optimistic claim is that algorithmic progress is a consequential additional source of progress. Treating any historical efficiency rate as a guaranteed exponential multiplier would go beyond the evidence.

## 3. Inference-time computation introduces another axis of improvement

This is arguably the most important addition to a case based on pretraining alone. A trained model can generate alternatives, critique intermediate steps, use tools, search, or select candidates with a verifier. Capability then depends on both what training installed and how much computation is available when solving a problem.

**Primary evidence:** Wang et al. (2023), [*Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.11171), sampled multiple reasoning paths and aggregated their final answers. They reported a 17.9-percentage-point improvement on GSM8K over chain-of-thought decoding in their evaluated setup. This measures a benchmark accuracy gain from a decoding procedure; it is not a comparable gain in general intelligence or a demonstration of lower total computational cost.

Lightman et al. (2023), [*Let's Verify Step by Step*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.20050), investigated process supervision and candidate selection on mathematical reasoning. Snell et al. (2024), [*Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally Can Be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.03314), studied how to allocate additional inference computation using revision and search with learned verification. Their results support task- and difficulty-dependent allocation rather than a universal rule that more generated tokens always help.

**Optimistic interpretation:** a model that sometimes produces a correct solution can become more useful if computation can reliably identify that solution. Search and verification may convert imperfect individual attempts into stronger system performance, allowing progress between major pretraining runs.

**Strong skeptical reply:** the conversion depends on candidate diversity and verifier quality. Correlated errors can defeat voting; a learned verifier can reward persuasive mistakes; open-ended projects often lack cheap, decisive correctness checks. More computation cannot reliably recover solutions outside the model's accessible search space.

**Assessment:** compelling evidence in verifiable domains, especially mathematics and programming; weaker evidence for broad, ambiguous, long-horizon work. The near-term case becomes stronger if reliable verification can itself be learned or supplied by interaction with the world.

## 4. Generalization gives scaling a plausible connection to breadth

**Primary evidence:** Brown et al. (2020), [*Language Models are Few-Shot Learners*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165), evaluated a pretrained language model across diverse tasks using instructions and examples in its context, without task-specific gradient updates during those evaluations. Wei et al. (2022), [*Finetuned Language Models Are Zero-Shot Learners*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.01652), showed that instruction tuning across a collection of tasks could improve performance on held-out task types.

**Optimistic interpretation:** a shared learning system acquires reusable representations and procedures rather than requiring a separate handcrafted solver for every task. That makes general competence a plausible continuation of demonstrated transfer, rather than a wholly unrelated target. Training on diverse tasks can also improve the ability to interpret new task instructions.

**Limits:** a held-out benchmark is not necessarily outside the distribution of pretraining knowledge or underlying task structures. Prompt sensitivity, contamination, memorization, and evaluation choices complicate claims about novelty. In-context adaptation also does not establish durable learning, robust causal understanding, or successful execution of unfamiliar projects.

The strongest case rests on transfer across multiple kinds of evaluation. It does not require claiming that every impressive answer demonstrates general reasoning.

## 5. Predictability and emergence can coexist

**Primary evidence:** the OpenAI (2023) [*GPT-4 Technical Report*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.08774) reports predicting aspects of final loss and coding performance using smaller training runs. This is evidence that some capability forecasting can work, but the report provides limited public information about training and is not an independently replicated forecasting program.

Schaeffer, Miranda, and Koyejo (2023), [*Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.15004), show that apparent discontinuities can arise from nonlinear or discrete evaluation metrics.

**Optimistic interpretation:** an ability need not undergo a mysterious internal phase transition to become economically useful abruptly. Smooth improvement in underlying success probabilities can cross a practical usability threshold. Thus, critiques of abrupt emergence do not by themselves undermine rapid practical progress.

**Skeptical qualification:** the location of an economically relevant threshold remains uncertain. A threshold in short-answer accuracy does not establish a threshold in dependable autonomy, where errors compound and recovery matters.

## Where the academic disagreement actually lies

The disagreement is less about whether scaling has worked than about whether its observed effects transfer to the remaining requirements for general intelligence. Optimists see a common learning substrate, repeated transfer, improving resource efficiency, and additional reasoning computation as mutually supporting evidence. Skeptics see an unvalidated bridge from those results to reliable learning and action in unfamiliar environments.

The optimistic case is strongest when presented as conditional: near-term AGI becomes more plausible if remaining weaknesses largely yield to feasible combinations of scale, interaction, search, and verification. The skeptical case is strongest when asking for direct evidence of that condition, rather than asserting permanent architectural impossibility.

These mechanisms should not be counted as independent pieces of evidence and multiplied together mechanically. Algorithmic efficiency changes scaling curves; inference-time search depends on pretrained competence; transfer results often share datasets and evaluation conventions. Nevertheless, their combination gives a stronger affirmative case than parameter-count extrapolation alone.

The most discriminating next evidence would be prospective forecasts evaluated on contamination-resistant, unfamiliar tasks, with total training and inference costs reported, and success measured over sustained work with error recovery. Existing studies support a credible route toward broader capability. They do not supply a calibrated probability or calendar date for AGI.

## 1. Definitions determine what the timeline predicts

There is no single accepted academic AGI endpoint.

- **General intelligence as adaptability across environments.** Legg and Hutter (2007), *Universal Intelligence: A Definition of Machine Intelligence*, formalize intelligence using performance across computable environments. This is a theoretical account, not a practical certification procedure. Broad benchmark success therefore does not directly establish this kind of generality.
- **Breadth and level of cognitive performance.** Morris et al. (2024), *Position: Levels of AGI for Operationalizing Progress on the Path to AGI*, distinguish generality, performance level, and autonomy. Their proposed Competent AGI level uses a threshold of at least the 50th percentile of skilled adults across a broad range of nonphysical tasks. That number is a stipulated classification threshold, not an empirical estimate that a particular system has attained it. Their inclusion of metacognitive abilities, including learning new skills, makes the target broader than examination performance.
- **Comprehensive task automation.** The expert-survey literature associated with Grace and colleagues asks about systems that can accomplish every task better and more cheaply than human workers, with the exact wording and assumptions varying across survey questions. This is an especially demanding endpoint. It should not be treated as equivalent to Morris et al.’s Competent AGI or to success on a finite benchmark collection.

The distinctions can move forecasts substantially. A broadly useful cognitive assistant, a reliable autonomous researcher, and a system capable of replacing workers throughout the economy are different forecast targets. Physical interaction, integration costs, and organizational adoption can delay economic replacement even after major cognitive advances.

“Near-term” is likewise not a standardized academic interval. A defensible forecast should state its origin date and deadline—for example, “by the end of 2030”—rather than using a rolling phrase such as “within a few years.” For the present discussion, “near-term” denotes approximately the next several years to a decade, as an analytical convention rather than an established definition.

## 2. What connects a scaling law to a timeline?

An AGI timeline implicitly combines several models:

**Calendar time → available resources and methods → learning performance → general capabilities → satisfaction of the chosen AGI criterion.**

Kaplan et al. (2020), *Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models*, and Hoffmann et al. (2022), *Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models*, principally inform the relationship between training resources and language-model loss. They do not estimate the whole chain.

A near-term forecast additionally assumes:

1. Sufficient compute, energy, capital, and suitable data will become available before the deadline.
2. Improvements in algorithms and resource allocation will continue, or at least will not be necessary beyond what is already demonstrated.
3. Lower loss, post-training, interaction, search, and tools will jointly improve the capabilities relevant to the AGI definition.
4. Critical weaknesses will yield to feasible interventions, without a new conceptual breakthrough whose arrival time is unknown.
5. Evaluation will reveal genuine competence on unfamiliar tasks rather than familiarity, contamination, or adaptation to the test.
6. The system can achieve the required reliability and autonomy at acceptable operating cost.

These assumptions are separable. Researchers can agree that loss scaling remains valid while disagreeing about any of the others.

## 5. Evidence against a forecast versus an unresolved question

A result is evidence against a near-term forecast when it is less expected under that forecast than under a plausible alternative.

- An anticipated capability improvement that repeatedly fails to appear after the forecast’s specified resource increases is adverse evidence.
- An observed resource constraint is adverse evidence if the forecast depends on exceeding it and lacks a supported substitute.
- A task failure is weakly diagnostic if both near-term and long-term views expected present systems to fail it.
- The absence of an accepted AGI test creates uncertainty; it does not by itself favor a later arrival date.
- An unexpectedly successful capability forecast supports the model that produced it, but only to the extent that the result discriminates between competing accounts.

This framing prevents both sides from treating every improvement or failure as decisive. It also requires optimism to specify expectations that could fail, and skepticism to specify improvements that would change its assessment.
